item.title: Elasto-Plastocapillarity: Surface-Tension-Driven Flows of Yield-Stress Fluids
item.description: arXiv:2610.33345v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this perspective article, we introduce elasto-plastocapillarity: surface-tension-driven free-surface flows of yield-stress fluids in which capillary stresses compete with yielding and elastic relaxation. We frame the relevant parameter space, and highlight representative problems (drops, bubbles, jets/filaments, thin films, and porous media) that are central to applications ranging from additive manufacturing and coatings to biological flows. We then outline a set of timely open challenges, including surface-tension measurements, breakdown of scale separation near the microstructures, coupled bulk-interface flow experimental diagnosis, interfacial rheology and surface stresses, history dependence, constitutive models and boundary conditions, reduced theoretical models, and the emerging opportunity provided by artificial intelligence and microgravity; aimed at guiding future experiments, theory, and computation.
item.dc:creator: Maziyar Jalaal

item.title: Mapping bimodal colloidal depletion systems onto the monodisperse gelation phase diagram
item.description: arXiv:2610.33394v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Many industries rely on models of colloidal gelation and phase behavior to predict how processing equipment will handle new product formulations. In colloidal systems with nearly uniform particle size it is possible to predict the formation of a gel from only three state variables; however, the extension of this model to bimodal and multimodal systems is not well described. Here we present a systematic simulation study of the attractive bimodal depletion gel phase diagram. For these systems, we find that gelation is highly dependent on total volume fraction, attraction conditions, and bimodal composition. Attraction and composition can be effectively collapsed into a single parameter using the contact-weighted second virial coefficient. This successfully projects the bimodal phase diagram onto the established monodisperse phase diagram, including accurately describing most bulk assembly properties; however, the underlying network structure of these gels remains highly dependent on the details of bimodal composition and attraction.
item.dc:creator: Robert A. Campbell, Ziye Zhuang, Ali Mohraz, Safa Jamali

item.title: Diffusion of chiral active Brownian particles in oscillatory Poiseuille flow
item.description: arXiv:2610.33466v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Micro- and nanoswimmers diffusing in a fluid flow confined to microchannels are often described by overdamped active Brownian particle dynamics, in which viscous effects dominate and inertia is negligible. Here, we investigate the diffusive behavior of chiral self-propelled particles in a two-dimensional microchannel with oscillatory Poiseuille flow. Using numerical simulations, we show that the effective diffusion coefficient strongly depends on the oscillation frequency, flow strength, intrinsic angular velocity, and rotational diffusion rate. Interestingly, the effective diffusion coefficient can oscillate with oscillation frequency and flow strength, exhibiting distinct maxima and minima. The enhanced diffusion peaks arise from resonant diffusion associated with the matching between the flow oscillation time scale and the intrinsic characteristic diffusion time scale. Moreover, we identify an additional vorticity matching mechanism, leading to alternating channel wall accumulation of particles during successive flow half-cycles. Additionally, chiral particles strongly amplify the resonant diffusion, producing diffusion enhancements of several orders of magnitude compared to nonchiral particles. The results of this study could have implications for controlling the diffusion of self-propelled particles in microfluidic channels using time-dependent flow.
item.dc:creator: Anshika Sharma, Vikas Sharma, Narender Khatri, Suneet Kumar Awasthi

item.title: Effect of Size Asymmetry and Zwitterionic Character of Solvent Ions on Impedance Spectra of Ultradilute Colloidal Suspensions
item.description: arXiv:2610.33541v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Buffer chemistry modulates colloidal impedance critically for label-free biosensing and electrokinetic diagnostics, yet classical models neglect buffer-specific interactions. We studied carboxylated polystyrene (PS) microspheres in conductivity-matched zwitterionic 4-(2-hydroxyethyl)-1-piperazineethanesulfonic acid (HEPES) and phosphate-buffered saline (PBS). Two concentration-dependent regimes emerged: oscillatory at ultradilute concentrations (<0.02 w/v%; Region 1) and monotonic at higher concentrations (Region 2). In Region 1, HEPES at pH 6.9 (approximately 80% zwitterionic) produced the largest deviation of delta Z from the O'Brien prediction. The conductivity increment was opposite in sign to classical expectation. We attribute this to zwitterion-driven interfacial ordering that enhances local conductivity and promotes self-limiting particle clustering. Dynamic light scattering detected cluster formation at 0.008 w/v%, well below aggregation thresholds. Changing pH from 6.9 to 8.1 strongly altered impedance amplitude; DLS profiles remained invariant. This indicates zwitterions modulate electrochemical polarization, not physical assembly. Molecular dynamics simulations showed pH-dependent HEPES organization at the PS surface. At pH 6.9, interfacial charge- and number-density profiles showed comparable oscillatory periodicity. At pH 8.1, anionic HEPES produced a more diffuse profile with increased Na+ compensation. These results support interfacial ordering as a contributor to enhanced conductivity but do not establish discrete layers or registry. Zeta potentials distinguished stable HEPES interfaces from PBS, where magnitude increased with ionic strength, contrary to classical screening theory. These nonlinear signatures and mesoscale organization underscore the role of buffer selection in high-sensitivity impedance biosensing.
item.dc:creator: Meenakshi, Shalini Gupta, Gaurav Goel

item.title: Aging dynamics and generalized superposition principles in carbon black-carboxymethylcellulose hydrogels
item.description: arXiv:2610.33682v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Aqueous dispersions of hydrophobic carbon black (CB) particles can be stabilized by carboxymethylcellulose (CMC), forming CB-CMC hydrogels whose microstructure is controlled by the relative CB-to-polymer content. At low CMC content, CB particles form a percolated, electrically conductive network, whereas at higher polymer content, CB particles act as isolated physical crosslinkers within an electrically insulating polymer matrix [see Legrand \textit{et al.}, Macromolecules 56, 2298-2308 (2023)]. Combining rheology and electrical impedance spectroscopy, we show that these two regimes exhibit markedly different aging dynamics. Conductive hydrogels exhibit logarithmic elastic recovery associated with a percolated CB network, whereas insulating hydrogels exhibit a combination of logarithmic and power-law stiffening, accompanied by dielectric polarization associated with confined ionic motion. The insulating hydrogels further exhibit a time-aging superposition principle, as their viscoelastic spectra measured in a time-resolved fashion can collapse onto a single master curve. Under steady shear, the viscoelastic response measured perpendicular to the flow also obeys a time--shear-rate superposition principle. Remarkably, the scaling between the shift factors under shear is reminiscent of critical-gel behavior, unlike that observed during aging at rest. Finally, time-resolved rheo-USAXS measurements performed during shear-rate cycles reveal structural rearrangements of CB particles and clusters that correlate with rheological hysteresis. These results provide a microstructural basis for understanding the nonlinear rheology of insulating CB-CMC hydrogels and establish generalized superposition principles as a unifying framework for their aging and flow behavior.
item.dc:creator: Gauthier Legrand, Guilhem P. Baeza, Jarno L. Waeterloos, Christian Clasen, S\'ebastien Manneville, Thibaut Divoux

item.title: Inverse origami inspired by insect morphogenesis: geometric design of wrinkle structures for curved surface formation
item.description: arXiv:2610.34903v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Insect exoskeletons abruptly acquire complex three-dimensional forms during metamorphosis from larva to pupa. This transformation occurs through the unfolding of preformed wrinkle structures inside the larval body under internal pressure. Inspired by this process, we investigate an inverse-origami strategy for fabricating curved surfaces. Whereas conventional origami produces three-dimensional objects by folding a flat sheet, this strategy produces curved surfaces by unfolding preformed wrinkle structures. The central design problem is to derive a wrinkle structure from a prescribed target surface. Our key idea is to regard a wrinkle structure as a unidirectional stretching field, which specifies at each point the stretch produced when the structure unfolds. We first derive such a field from the target surface geometry and then translate it into spatially varying wrinkle directions and spacing, so that the wrinkle structure unfolds into the target. The resulting numerical designs approximate the intrinsic metric of the target surface. We demonstrate the method on multiple target surfaces through numerical construction, mechanical unfolding simulations, and 3D-printed prototypes. This work provides a biologically inspired geometric design principle for encoding prescribed surface shapes in wrinkle structures, as well as a framework for designing and fabricating deployable curved surfaces.
item.dc:creator: Kentaro Morikawa, Yuuki Shimizu, Nen Saito, Yasuhiro Inoue

item.title: Interfacial bacteria-driven rotation of free-floating active droplets
item.description: arXiv:2610.35242v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Active droplets provide a platform for converting microscopic propulsion into macroscopic flow. Previous realizations of bacteria-driven droplet rotation typically rely on nearby solid boundaries, external fields, or dense active nematics. Here, we report autonomous rotation of droplets in a three-dimensional aqueous two-phase system driven by interfacial population of \textit{Pseudomonas aeruginosa}. Combining confocal microscopy with fluid particle dynamics simulations, we show that amphiphilic bacteria accumulate at the dextran--polyethylene glycol interface and preferentially move and orient along the local tangent. Interfacial localization partitions the force-free swimming dipole between the two liquid phases, allowing either phase to experience a finite active torque while the combined system remains torque balanced. The simulated interfacial population is more spatially heterogeneous than in the experiments, emphasizing that both the bacterial distribution and its signed orientational organization can influence the instantaneous torque. Over the accessible size range, the macroscopic angular velocity exhibits an inverse-radius ($R^{-1}$) dependence. We also formulate a theoretical model to rationalize this scaling law, revealing how the macroscopic rotation is governed by collective interfacial swimming and surface coverage. These results identify a fluid-interface-mediated route for converting swimmer activity into macroscopic rotational flow and establish a strategy for harnessing interfacial active matter to regulate droplet dynamics.
item.dc:creator: Dixi Yang, Anheng Wang, Chunming Wang, Hajime Tanaka, Jiaxing Yuan

item.title: Synchronization-controlled transport near an absorbing transition: Effective Enskog kinetic theory of a driven granular monolayer
item.description: arXiv:2610.35270v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Synchronization with vibrating boundaries can qualitatively alter the dynamics of confined granular fluids and control the collision-induced transfer of energy to horizontal motion. We develop an Enskog kinetic theory for the active phase of a driven granular monolayer within the framework of the $\Delta$-model, which accounts for the transfer of energy from the vertical to the horizontal degrees of freedom of grains. Synchronization effects are incorporated through a state-dependent effective collision rule governed by the interplay between the local collision frequency and a characteristic synchronization time. A viscous drag force is also included to account for energy dissipation arising from interactions with the confining plates. Within this framework, we characterize the homogeneous active state and use it as the reference state for a Chapman--Enskog expansion. The solution of the Enskog equation to Navier--Stokes order then yields explicit expressions for the shear and bulk viscosities, the thermal conductivity, the diffusive heat coefficient, and the first-order contribution to the cooling rate, consistently accounting for inelasticity, damping, finite-density effects, and synchronization. Event-driven molecular-dynamics simulations show that the theory accurately describes the steady temperature and shear and bulk viscosities over a broad region of the active phase. Close to the discontinuous synchronization-controlled absorbing transition, deviations are mainly attributed to the mean-field coarse-graining of the microscopic synchronization dynamics: fluctuations of the collision-dependent injection amplitude and correlations between synchronization and pre-collisional velocities become increasingly important. These results provide a kinetic description of synchronization-controlled transport and delineate its range of validity near the absorbing transition.
item.dc:creator: David Gonz\'alez M\'endez, Rub\'en G\'omez Gonz\'alez, Rapha\"{e}l Maire, Vicente Garz\'o, Ignacio Pagonabarraga

item.title: Rigid Particle-Induced Anomalous Softening in Elastomer Composites
item.description: arXiv:2610.35380v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Particle-filled soft composites generally stiffen as particle loading increases, imposing a trade-off between functionality and compliance. Here, we show that this trade-off can be overcome by designing particles to actively direct gelation rather than act as passive fillers. In a sol-rich elastomer matrix, sol-phase kinetics redirect network formation towards particle-mediated assembly, yielding anomalous softening despite increasing particle content. This response is governed by topological reconfiguration of the load-bearing network during gelation rather than by filler loading alone. A structure-based model captures the composition-dependent onset of this behaviour, and the same response is reproduced across distinct particle systems. The resulting materials combine functionality with softness, energy dissipation, and recoverability under large deformation. These findings establish topology-guided gelation as a general strategy for engineering compliant functional composites for soft robotic actuation, conformal interfaces, and other systems that require both deformability and embedded material functionality.
item.dc:creator: Yonghyun Cho, Hyeongho Min, Hongdeok Kim, Dongeun Lee, Minjune Kim, Siyeon Jang, Ali Amini, Zitang Wei, Hosub Lim, Hwan-ho Cho, Bo-yong Park, Sang Won Lee, Joonmyung Choi, Metin Sitti, Sangyul Baik

item.title: A Universal Constitutive Relation for Static Droplet Retention
item.description: arXiv:2610.33100v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Under applied forcing, static droplet retention is accompanied by contact angle asymmetry, with unequal apparent contact angles on opposite sides. Yet, the relation between the asymmetry and forcing lacks a common constitutive basis. Here, we show that the asymmetry emerges from minimizing the forcing-dependent free energy. The response of the asymmetry to forcing defines a susceptibility whose zero-forcing value yields a universal constitutive relation between the asymmetry and forcing. The constitutive relation is quantitatively validated across liquids, volumes, and forcing levels.
item.dc:creator: Lisen Bi, Fei Wang, Ruize Yin, Britta Nestler

item.title: A neural accelerated surface-roughness-based Discrete Element Method (SR-DEM) for modeling granular systems
item.description: arXiv:2610.33363v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The Discrete Element Method (DEM) is an indispensable tool for modeling and understanding the basic mechanical behaviors of (dry) granular media, a class of disordered material systems of significant interest to multiple scientific domains from (geo-)physics to (chemical) engineering. At the core of all present DEM frameworks is a phenomenological friction law--commonly chosen to be of the Amontons-Coulomb type--that models the frictional interaction among constituent grains. Here, inspired by research in the tribology community, we present an alternative, fundamentally different framework, termed surface-roughness-based DEM (SR-DEM), in which contact friction is handled in a more physics-based manner. In this framework, instead of using a friction law, we explicitly resolve the surface topography of each grain and let friction emerge from collective frictionless interactions of surface asperities. In essence, we trade phenomenology for physics at the cost of an increased computational demand. To mitigate the cost, we introduce an FE$^2$-like algorithm and a feature-wise linear modulation (FiLM)-based neural network surrogate, both of which are parallelized on GPU to accelerate contact computation. Crucially, using this framework in 2D, we (1) demonstrate the possibility of recovering a two-body-based Amontons-Coulomb-type friction behavior using a simple representation of surface topography, and (2) identify many-body-based frictional behaviors--more specifically, the angle of repose values--that cannot always be captured by current DEM frameworks under the same level of model complexity. We conclude by discussing future directions for SR-DEM, as well as exciting new opportunities it could unlock for a wide range of emerging applications, including (designing) suspension rheology and metamaterial mechanics.
item.dc:creator: Xiwei Pan, Liuchi Li

item.title: kstress: a LAMMPS package for calculating the 2D wavevector-dependent stress tensor and its anisotropy in amorphous solids
item.description: arXiv:2610.34206v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The stress tensor resolved in wavevector $\qvec$ and time $t$, $\sigma_{\alpha\beta}(\qvec,t)$, gives access to the elastic moduli of amorphous solids as a function of the probed length scale, and to the long-range stress correlations that distinguish an amorphous solid from a liquid. Its evaluation requires the contribution of every interacting pair and therefore an interface to the force loop of the molecular dynamics code. In the current work, we present: i) an optimized implementation of the LAMMPS~\cite{lammps} module for calculating $\sigma_{\alpha\beta}(\qvec,t)$, in which trigonometric functions are calculated only for the basic wavevectors and, in addition, all the relevant wavevectors are supplied as an explicit list rather than generated as a full grid, so that only the wavevectors of interest are computed and stored, and ii) a validation protocol for the code illustrated for a two-dimensional polydisperse Lennard-Jones (2DpLJ) glass-forming liquid. Based on these technical achievements we elucidated how the affine moduli for the 2DpLJ model depend on the norm $q$ of the wavevector. In particular, we demonstrate that the longitudinal affine modulus shows a minimum near $q_\text{max}$ corresponding to the main peak of the structure factor. Our data also point to the peaks in the $q$-dependencies of vibrational frequencies well below $q_\text{max}$ for both transverse and longitudinal modes. The potential relevance of this feature to the ``boson peak'' is discussed as well.
item.dc:creator: Olivier Benzerara, J\"org Baschnagel, Alexander N. Semenov, Liudmyla Klochko

item.title: Theoretical description of high-harmonic spectroscopy for uniaxial nematic and isotropic liquid crystals
item.description: arXiv:2610.35672v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Enabled by their controllable optical anisotropy, liquid crystals form a cornerstone of linear optical and display technologies. Bringing the versatile platform into the nonlinear regime, we explore its nonlinear optical anisotropy by high-order harmonic generation spectroscopy. Through a comprehensive study targeting gas, liquid, nematic, and crystalline phases, we present a semi-empirical tight-binding approach that provides insight into the intermolecular character of ultrafast light-driven electron dynamics across soft-matter mesophases. We demonstrate how intermolecular electron hybridization enables spectroscopic access to structural properties, such as the nematic director and order parameter. Outlining such foundational mechanisms opens avenues towards nonlinear liquid crystal devices and ultrafast soft-matter spectroscopies.
item.dc:creator: Simon Vendelbo Bylling Jensen, Marta L. Murillo-S\'anchez, Andrea Annunziata, Angel Rubio, Laura Cattaneo, Nicolas Tancogne-Dejean

item.title: Multiscale dynamics in yield stress fluids during homogeneous and shear-banded yielding
item.description: arXiv:2402.00221v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Whether homogeneous and shear-banded yielding involve distinct microscopic mechanisms remains unresolved. We combine oscillatory rheology with gradient-resolved particle tracking to compare a ductile Carbopol microgel that yields homogeneously with a more brittle dense emulsion that develops stationary shear bands. In both systems, we separate long-range correlated ballistic flow from local Fickian diffusion and find that the two act on the same tracers, rather than on distinct persistent populations. This finding challenges the distinct-population interpretation of earlier experiments, which could access only dynamics averaged over particles and along the velocity-gradient direction. We distinguish these contributions in Carbopol by varying the tracer radius $a$ and the observation-window size $L$ independently. The ballistic velocity is independent of $a$ but increases with $L$, indicating correlations beyond the field of view; the diffusion coefficient $D$ scales as $1/a$ and is independent of $L$. At fixed driving frequency and tracer size, emulsion measurements collapse onto a single $D(\gamma_L)$ curve, whether taken across the banded profile or at fixed height under varying applied amplitude. Local strain amplitude, rather than stress, therefore governs the mean diffusive mobility within our resolution. The increase of $D$ with $\gamma_L$ is steeper than in Carbopol, consistent with the emulsion's greater brittility. Diffusive displacements are nearly Gaussian in Carbopol, with no measurable cooperativity, while in the emulsion they are strongly non-Gaussian and cooperative. There, the four-point susceptibility is largest at the strain characterising the interband region. Homogeneous and shear-banded yielding therefore share the same dynamical ingredients, while differing in the statistics and spatial organisation of the residual diffusive motion.
item.dc:creator: P. Edera, M. Brizioli, M. Madani, E. Ngouamba, P. Coussot, V. Trappe, G. Petekidis, F. Giavazzi, R. Cerbino

item.title: Active motility and wetting cooperatively regulate liquid-liquid phase separation
item.description: arXiv:2511.18077v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Liquid--liquid phase separation in aqueous two-phase systems is widespread in physical and biological settings, yet how motile agents regulate its morphology and kinetics remains poorly understood. Combining experiments on \textit{Pseudomonas aeruginosa} in a dextran--polyethylene glycol mixture with hydrodynamic simulations, we show that interfacial wetting couples bacterial motility to phase-separation dynamics. At high dextran fraction, bacteria-driven rotational flows shear inter-droplet gaps and hinder liquid-bridge formation, thereby suppressing coalescence and coarsening. As the dextran fraction decreases, wetting-driven bridging becomes increasingly important, producing an intermediate chain-like state and, ultimately, branched bacterial clusters in which activity instead accelerates capture and aggregation. A biofilm-associated protein provides an independent wetting component that similarly promotes bacterial clustering. These results reveal a composition-controlled crossover between activity-induced suppression of coalescence and wetting-dominated bridging.
item.dc:creator: Dixi Yang, Anheng Wang, Chunming Wang, Hajime Tanaka, Jiaxing Yuan

item.title: Stress Relaxation Driven by Elementary Plastic Events in Non-Ageing Liquid Foams
item.description: arXiv:2602.23690v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Liquid foams are archetypal athermal amorphous solids whose elasticity arises from the jamming of densely packed bubbles. We investigate the stress relaxation of non-ageing liquid foams following flow cessation, using fast X-ray tomo-rheoscopy. Thanks to in situ, time-resolved measurements, we uncover robust linear affine relationships between shear stress, plastic activity, and coordination number throughout the relaxation toward a residual stress state below the yield value. In contrast to previous studies on amorphous solids, we observe an exponential relaxation governed by the duration of individual plastic events, rather than by cascades of correlated ones associated with much longer, shear-rate-dependent timescales or power-law relaxations. Our results provide new insight into the microscopic mechanisms governing the time evolution of stress in jammed amorphous solids.
item.dc:creator: F. Schott, B. Dollet, C. M. Schlep\"utz, C. Claudet, S. Gst\"ohl, R. Mokso, S. Santucci, C. Raufaste

item.title: The fluid-lattice gas isomorphism with application to liquid-vapor equilibrium in physisorbed monolayers
item.description: arXiv:2606.08178v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Liquid-gas equilibrium is described using a pair of Ising-like thermodynamic variables. The first is a combination of density and energy fields that is even under phase coexistence, derived from the Gibbs-Duhem and Clausius-Clapeyron relations. The second is the normalized density deviation $M=\rho/\rho_d-1$, which distinguishes the coexisting phases and serves as an odd ordering variable. Combining these variables with the empirical linearities of the binodal diameter and the Zeno line leads to a projective mapping between continuum-fluid and lattice-gas states. The implications of such mapping are tested against coexistence-density and saturation pressure data for the two-dimensional Lennard-Jones fluid, as well as physisorbed molecular monolayers of simple molecular fluids like argon and methane. Finally, a heuristic microscopic interaction-variable formulation that motivates continuous fluids versus lattice model description is also discussed.
item.dc:creator: Lev Shevchenko, Volodymyr Kulinskii

item.title: Geometric formulation of state-dependent Langevin dynamics using scalar free energy
item.description: arXiv:2606.13617v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Stochastic dynamics with state-dependent diffusion arise broadly in confined, anisotropic, and hydrodynamically coupled systems. The conventional Langevin equation contains a spurious drift associated with multiplicative noise. Since the restricted free energy is generally non-scalar, the covariance is not explicit. Here, we reformulate state-dependent Langevin dynamics using a scalar free energy and a diffusion metric defined by the inverse diffusion tensor. The conventional spurious drift is then expressed as a Christoffel contribution. Although our formulation is mathematically equivalent to the conventional one through the relation between the restricted and scalar free energies, it makes coordinate covariance explicit and enables the phenomenological construction of thermodynamic potentials directly from system symmetries. We demonstrate its consistency in representative examples of state-dependent diffusion arising from coordinate transformations, geometric confinement, and projection from curved to flat spaces.
item.dc:creator: Kento Yasuda, Zhongqiang Xiong, Zhanglin Hou, Kenta Ishimoto, Xinpeng Xu, Shigeyuki Komura

item.title: Precipitation-dissolution cycling drives intermittent salt creeping
item.description: arXiv:2607.11587v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Salt creeping --- the precipitation of salt crystals away from an evaporating liquid interface along surrounding surfaces --- occurs across settings from geology and cultural-heritage weathering to inkjet printing and carbon sequestration. Yet why its dynamics are sometimes smooth and sometimes violently intermittent has remained unexplained. Here we investigate the confined evaporation of salt solutions from a capillary with unidirectional water loss, and show that intermittent salt creeping is driven by a cycle of precipitation and dissolution sustained entirely by liquid transport. Time-resolved measurements reveal that each burst of crystal growth coincides with episodic imbibition of solution into the growing salt deposit on the outer capillary surface, which couples evaporation to crystallization. Combining experiments with a minimal theoretical model, we show that the difference between the supersaturation at which crystals nucleate and the saturation concentration at which they redissolve --- the metastable zone of the salt --- is sufficient to generate this cycle. The same mechanism accounts for the cases in which creeping is not intermittent: where the concentration at the capillary exit never reaches the nucleation threshold the liquid meniscus recedes smoothly, and where it cannot subsequently fall back below saturation the deposit grows continuously, exhibiting self-amplified creeping. Our results recast salt creeping as a relaxation oscillator, and identify precipitation-dissolution cycling as a generic route to intermittency in evaporating multicomponent fluids.
item.dc:creator: Javier Rodr\'iguez-Rodr\'iguez, Manikuntala Mukhopadhyay, Lijun Thayyil Raju, Detlef Lohse, Jasper van der Gucht, Uddalok Sen

item.title: A closed-form theory of charge-regulated electrostatic interactions between anisotropically charged spheres
item.description: arXiv:2608.30566v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Proteins and many other colloids carry ionizable surface groups that are both spatially inhomogeneous (patchy) and pH-responsive (charge-regulating). In the description of the electrostatic interactions between such particles, these two aspects are often treated separately, especially from a theoretical perspective. We present a unified, closed-form theory that unites charge regulation and patchiness within the linearized Poisson--Boltzmann approximation. For spherical particles with anisotropic distributions of titratable sites, we derive both the leading-order mean-field interaction energy as well as the Kirkwood--Shumaker fluctuation interaction. The theory exposes a qualitatively new effect between two electroneutral anisotropic particles: proximity-induced charge regulation generates a net monopole, and splits orientational branches that are {mirror-symmetric} in any linear fixed-charge model. The accompanying correction to the interaction energy has no fixed sign---it weakens like-charge repulsion but can deepen an existing attraction or create one where fixed charge predicts none. We benchmark three components of the theory against published results, as no existing simulation probes their combination, which would capture the central prediction of the theory. Lastly, we apply the theory to two proteins---lysozyme and $\alpha$-chymotrypsinogen A---and show that it not only reproduces the general trends of the measured second virial coefficients but also predicts how charge regulation expands the range of pH and screening strength where the protein--protein interaction is attractive.
item.dc:creator: An\v{z}e Bo\v{z}i\v{c}

item.title: Maximum Velocity of a Liquid Metal Drop Driven by a Time-Dependent Electrocapillary Excitation
item.description: arXiv:2512.20516v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Gallium alloys are promising materials in biomedical engineering, electronics, and wireless communications, thanks to their good conductivity, non toxicity and their ability to sustain large deformations. They can be transported in capillaries using purely electric means by continuous electrowetting (CEW). Current models of CEW-driven flows do not address the transient response to fast changes in the excitation, crucial in many applications. Here, we present a theory that describes the CEW-driven oscillatory motion of a drop of Eutectic Gallium-Indium alloy inside a capillary. We consider inertia, viscosity and the transient response of the electrical circuit consisting of the drop plus the electrolyte where it is immersed. The theory describes fairly well the experimental drop velocity and explains the existence of an optimal frequency that maximizes the velocity.
item.dc:creator: Javier Otero Martinez, Ana Garcia Armada, Yi Li, Christian Nijhuis, Javier Rodr\'iguez-Rodr\'iguez
